## What this paper contributes — the innovation, stated so it can be checked
Each claim below names where it is enforced or measured. "First" is used only where a prior instance would falsify it.

1. The quote and the execution are one computation. The route is derived inside the transaction that executes it, from public pool state, by a stateless library any reader can re-run, and the number that binds at settlement is re-derived by the same dispatcher in the executing frame (§2, §11). There is no routing service, no price oracle, no keeper and no upgrade path — the dependency budget is the empty set (§3, INV-3, INV-4).
2. Metrological Design, the discipline behind every mechanism: measure every coordinate that can be measured, and make the rest monotone so that a false input hurts only its supplier (§2). It is why the fee base is a measured balance and never a declared one (INV-15), why a caller can tighten protection but never loosen it (INV-5), and why a venue that cannot be bounded is surrendered rather than guessed (INV-14).
3. Uniswap V4 end to end, in-frame: to our knowledge the first router to derive, prove, price, screen and settle V4 pools entirely inside the executing transaction — pools without addresses, hooks screened by their address bits before any call is made (E18, INV-11), dynamic fees read live (E19), native-currency pools included (§5).
4. Deterministic Derivation 𝒟: a pool address is computed, not fetched, wherever the arithmetic allows (E8, §7); an address that can be derived can be proven, and every pool that enters the registry proves it trades the pair (INV-19).
5. The Monoslot: a pool's entire routing state in one 256-bit word, read once and decoded by pure arithmetic (E9, §8) — the reason the executor measures 2.4–10.9× less gas per leg than the sector's leading router (§17).
6. The Self-Healing Registry and the Vitality Field Ψ: the registry learns liquidity by trading it, ranks venues by a field that decays by arithmetic (E10–E13), holds at most sixteen pools per pair and evicts by fitness (INV-8), with no indexer and no keeper (§9). Ψ ranks and truncates; nothing that prices a trade reads it (INV-7).
7. The Iron-Law floor Φ and the Surplus Rule: the floor is computed from measured quantities and compiled in (E15, E16), the protocol fee and its split are constants without setters (E17, INV-4), and execution surplus is returned to the user (§11, §13). Nobody — the authors included — can change the fee or the floors after deployment.
8. One fee, charged once, on a measured base: the two regimes and the Surplus Rule (E26, INV-20), resistant to fee-on-transfer tokens, stray balances and a lied-about route total (§13).
9. The verification apparatus is printed with its denominators (§15): a curated mutation guard where every mutant is killed by its named test (203 of 203), regime covering arrays of strength 2 and 3 (all 258 pairs, all 1,636 triples), N-version testing of the quote mathematics at three optimiser settings, 14 + 5 metamorphic relations, fee-mutant detection with a Wilson 95 % interval, and a 240-sample study of how a quote ages. We know of no other public DeFi codebase that publishes a curated mutation guard with per-mutant killing tests, a strength-3 covering array over its regime factors, N-version testing of its quote maths, or the detection rate of its own fee mutants with a confidence interval; the artefacts are in the repository, so a prior instance would falsify the claim.
10. The paper is written to be cited by object: 26 primitive equations (E1–E26) and 22 enforced invariants (INV-1–INV-22) with stable identifiers, each tied to the function that implements it, and reproduction commands for every figure (Appendix C).

## The architecture in one screen
Five contracts, trust running one way (§16). The Core is pure mathematics — the Eightfold Dispatcher Ω (E2–E7, §4), derivation (E8), the Monoslot (E9), Ψ (E10–E13), the floor (E15, E23) — imported by the other four, so one audit of the mathematics covers every consumer. The Hub is the registry: it learns pools from settled swaps (recordSwap, onlyRouter), proves the pair before admitting one (INV-19), and answers three facts a route needs — is this token a bridge, is this hook live, the registration write — and nothing that prices a trade. The Solver is a stateless library that derives the route in-frame: candidates by Ψ, believability by depth-weighted median (E25), the Split Allocator across pools of the same pair (E14), up to three hops and four legs per hop (INV-18). The Router is the only contract that moves funds and holds none between transactions (INV-1): it re-prices every leg in the executing frame, enforces the effective minimum (E16) and the aggregate hop floor (E24), screens hooks by address (E18), charges the fee once on a measured base (E17, E26), pays the surplus to the user, and settles atomically or not at all (INV-2). The Quoter is a read-only preview surface whose gap to the in-frame path is measured, not assumed (§12, E21). Every contract ships under the 24,000-byte gate on the release profile (INV-22).

## Abstract
BlazePhoenix-Dex is an on-chain liquidity aggregator built on one claim: a quote and its execution are the same computation. The route is derived inside the transaction that executes it, from public pool state, by a stateless library any reader can re-run; the number that binds at settlement is re-derived by the same dispatcher in the executing frame. There is no routing service, no price oracle, no keeper and no upgrade path. This paper specifies the five contracts — Core, Hub, Solver, Router, Quoter — and the operators of the Meta-Equation: the Eightfold Dispatcher Ω, the Deterministic Derivation 𝒟, the Iron-Law floor Φ, the Vitality Field Ψ and the anti-scam projector Ξ. Behind them sits one discipline, Metrological Design: measure every coordinate that can be measured, and make the rest monotone so a false input hurts only its supplier. Every guarantee is stated with its enforcement site and its limit. The verification apparatus is printed with its denominators: 1,319 of 1,320 tests green on the release profile, 203 of 203 curated mutants killed, 14 of 15 mutants aimed at 43 stateful invariants noticed, covering arrays of strength 2 (63 rows, 258 pairs) and 3 (168 rows, 1,636 triples), 14 + 5 metamorphic relations, three optimiser builds in agreement, and a 240-sample study of how a quote ages. What none of it establishes is stated as carefully. The code described is V2 and is not deployed; the deployed generation is V1, pinned by codehash so the two are never conflated.

## Status
The Version 2 tree this paper describes is in the repository and is not deployed; the deployed generation is Version 1, pinned by codehash on every network so the two are never conflated. Every number in the paper is measured on main 8949a9d and printed beside its denominator; full text in English at https://blazephoenix.xyz/whitepaper.md.

    repository — a prior instance would falsify the claim.

## What the paper does NOT establish (state these as carefully as the record)
- The Version 2 code is not deployed; the deployed generation is Version 1, pinned by codehash. Do not describe V2 as live.
- No independent external audit has been completed (planned before launch). "Audited" is the wrong word; "measured in public, with a funded bounty, pending external audit" is the accurate one.
- MEV ordering is not eliminated — ordering is decided before contract code runs; the paper measures the bound (the sandwich curve of §14.3), it does not claim immunity.
- The curated mutation guard is adequate against its mutant set; it is not a proof of the absence of defects (§15.11).

## Section digest — the opening paragraph of each of the 24 sections
§1 The problem: a quote is a promise someone else computed
  Imagine selling a car in a city with twenty dealers. A good broker visits all twenty, finds the best price, and perhaps splits the sale across two of them. Most on-chain "brokers" check prices on their own database — possibly stale — and show you a result. You cannot verify that they looked at all twenty, or that they showed you the best one. You can only verify that they have, so far, been honest.
§2 The answer and the discipline
  BlazePhoenix-Dex has an entry point that takes six values — the two tokens, the amount, your minimum, a recipient, a deadline — and works out the route inside the transaction that executes it, from pool reserves that are public state: which venues, how much to each, in what order. Because the route was derived from public state by public code, anyone can re-derive it.
§3 The Meta-Equation and the dependency budget
  The whole aggregator can be read as the maximisation of one expression. Given an input token t_in, an output token t_out and an amount x, the Solver searches the admissible routes for the one maximising net received value, subject to a feasibility floor and an anti-scam gate.
§4 The Eightfold Dispatcher Ω
  Plain: one function that knows how to price every kind of pool. Precise: universalQuote(QuoteCtx, amountIn) in the Core is the quote dispatcher for the Solver and for the Quoter's preview; it returns the expected output and a token-denominated depth for the split allocator, and a pool it cannot price returns zero and is dropped before anything is sent.
§5 Uniswap V4 end to end
  Uniswap V4 is not a new pool contract; it is a new shape of venue, and it invalidates four assumptions every router built between 2020 and 2024 rests on. Pools have no addresses — they are entries in one singleton's storage, keyed by a hash. Arbitrary code runs inside the swap — a hook executes at defined points of the settlement the router is performing. Fees need not be constant. And pools may hold the chain's native currency, which has no balanceOf. This section answers all four structurally, so that a V4 leg is — to the Solver, to the floors and to the trader — indistinguishable from any other leg.
§6 The Solidly solver
  Some invariants have no closed form simple enough to reproduce safely, and reproducing them is exactly the replication risk the protocol refuses elsewhere. For such venues the dispatcher asks the pool, through the narrowest honest channel the venue exposes — and holds a replica in reserve for forks that do not answer.
§7 Deterministic Derivation 𝒟
  Before a pool can be quoted it must be found. The industry's answer is to ask: a call to the venue's factory reads a storage mapping and returns an address, and the caller takes the factory's word. BlazePhoenix supports that answer — four factory-call modes cover the venues whose deployments are not reproducible — and prefers a stronger one wherever the arithmetic allows: compute the address, with no external call. An address that is computed can be verified by anyone with the same three inputs; an address that is fetched can only be trusted.
§8 The Monoslot
  Storage is the dominant cost of doing anything on the EVM: a cold SLOAD is 2,100 gas, and a registry that scattered a pool's attributes across separate slots would pay it again for every attribute, for every pool, on every route evaluated. BlazePhoenix packs a pool's entire routing state into a single 256-bit word — the Monoslot — read once and decoded by pure arithmetic.
§9 The Self-Healing Registry and the Vitality Field Ψ
  Most aggregators know their venues because a keeper indexes pools off-chain and pushes lists on-chain — a trusted process, a staleness window and an operational dependency, three things a protocol that solves routes on-chain cannot accept. BlazePhoenix takes the opposite stance: the registry learns liquidity by trading it.
§10 Routing and the Split Allocator
  A constant-product pool prices by one rule: its two reserves, multiplied, may never shrink. Pour Δ in with fee retention γ (a 0.30 % venue fee means γ = 0.997) and you receive yγΔ / (x + γΔ), with your own input in the denominator: the more you push through one pool, the worse each further token pays. Slippage is arithmetic, and so is its cure: splitting the same order across pools of the same pair moves each pool less.
§11 The execution layer and the Iron-Law floor Φ
  The Solver proposes; the Router disposes — atomically, or not at all. The Router is the only contract that moves funds, holds none between transactions, and is built on one principle: one mechanism per concern, applied universally. It assumes nothing it can measure.
§12 Quote surfaces, and how a quote ages
  There are two places a number called "your quote" can come from, and they are different code paths: the Quoter, a read-only preview contract an interface calls before you sign, and the in-frame path, where the Solver and Router compute quotes inside the executing transaction. §4.4 gave the per-kind truth; this section gives the surfaces and measures the gap between them.
§13 Fee policy: the two regimes and the Surplus Rule
  Plain: the protocol takes 0.28 % once, from one measured amount, in a coin the treasury wants to hold, and counts that it did. Precise: PROTOCOL_FEE_BPS = 28 is a compile-time constant in the Core with no setter anywhere in the deployed bytecode; the fee is mulDivUp(base, 28, 10,000) — rounded up, so a zero fee is unreachable for any non-zero base — split TREASURY1_SHARE = 3,000 bps to the first treasury and the remainder to the second (computed as fee − t1, so the two always sum to the fee with no dust), the treasuries fixed at construction and freezable for ever by the One-Way Door.
§14 Security model
  Plain: the Router holds nothing between transactions, every swap is all-or-nothing, and each attack class this repository has considered is answered by a named check or named as out of scope. Precise: the threat catalogue is docs/assurance/threats.json, 23 classes drawn from the public record of exploits; each names the guard symbol that refuses it, and a CI script fails the build if the symbol leaves src/ or the named test leaves test/. Coverage of a catalogue is a floor on what has been considered, never a ceiling on what exists.
§15 The verification apparatus, measured
  Plain: every number here is printed beside the denominator it was measured against, is recomputed from a clean checkout by a script or a named forge command (Appendix C), and is followed by what it does not establish. Precise: the tree measured is main at 8949a9d and the branch that became it, on the release profile (optimizer_runs = 300, via_ir), 2026-09-05.
§16 Architecture and sizes
  Plain: five contracts, one of which is pure mathematics imported by the other four, and no piece of mathematics is defined twice. Precise: the Core is a stateless library with no storage, no owner and no upgrade path; Hub, Solver, Router and Quoter import it and none redefines a primitive, so one audit of the mathematics covers every consumer.
§17 Measured performance
  Plain: everything in this section was measured on forks of real chains — real venues, real reserves deposited by strangers, one bytecode — and is labelled as exactly that. Precise: a number appears here only if a public harness in the repository reproduces it; the harness, the chain and the date are printed beside it. A fork measurement is evidence about behaviour, not a deployment record; the deployment record is §19. The measurements of §12 and §15 are from 2026-09-05; the campaign of this section was run in August 2026 and its harnesses are in test/fork/.
§18 The second engine, by reference
  BlazePhoenix's token is designed to work, not to sit still. A staking engine for BZPX — a single-asset vault in which collateral, reward and accounting are one token and solvency is a revert condition on every value-moving transaction — is specified in full in its own paper, BlazePhoenix Staking Engine — Design Specification, Version 1.0 (https://blazephoenix.xyz/staking-whitepaper.md), on its own track, and is under construction. This paper deliberately does not summarise it: its emission mechanics, its accounting identities and its own edges are specified there.
§19 Deployment status
  This paper documents the repository, and the repository is canonical: where this text and the source disagree, the source wins. Two generations exist and they are never conflated.
§20 Token — BZPX
  One billion BZPX, fixed for ever, as a plain ERC-20: 18 decimals, no mint path, no fee-on-transfer, no rebasing, no transfer hooks, no pause or blacklist — the six deploy invariants recorded in the staking repository and checked against the token bytecode at wiring time. Fully-diluted supply is known from genesis; scarcity is a property of the contract, not a policy.
§21 Research programme and security record
  Before this project had a research programme worth the name, independent researchers read the source hostilely — unasked, with nothing promised — and disclosed what they saw privately. The code this paper describes is the code that survived their reading. What each of them reported, and what became of it, lives where such records belong: in the repository's SECURITY.md and SECURITY_HALL_OF_FAME.md, next to the code, where every entry can be checked in both directions. This section records who they are, what hostile reading pays, and the shape of what it found.
§22 What you must trust, and what you need not
  Every protocol claims to be trustless; almost none can enumerate its exceptions. Here is the full list, each power stated with the line that bounds it.
§23 Related work
  Routing. Angeris, Evans, Chitra and Boyd cast routing across constant-function market makers as a convex program whose optimum equalises marginal prices across venues; Diamandis, Resnick, Chitra and Angeris give an efficient dual-decomposition algorithm for it.
§24 Conclusion
  We set out to build an aggregator on one discipline — measure, do not believe — and to hold it at every point where a number could instead have been taken on someone's word: the route, the price, the floor, the fee base, the venue set, the pair a pool claims to trade, even the protocol's own cost model.

## Appendix A — the primitive equations (E1–E26), each implemented once at the site named
E1 · Meta-Equation · $R^{\star} = \arg\max_{R}\ \mathrm{net}(R)\cdot\prod_{\ell}\hat{\Psi}(p_{\ell})\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{net}(R)\ge\Phi(R)]\cdot\Xi(R)$ · defined in Solver pipeline · §3
E2 · Constant-product output · $y = \lfloor x(\mathrm{BPS}-f)\,r_{\mathrm{out}} / (r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm{BPS} + x(\mathrm{BPS}-f)) \rfloor$ · defined in Core `outV2` · §4.2
E3 · Concentrated-liquidity output (within tick) · $\sqrt{P}' = L\sqrt{P}/(L + x_{f}\sqrt{P}/Q_{96})$, $y = L(\sqrt{P}-\sqrt{P}')/Q_{96}$; dual form for the other direction · defined in Core `outV3` · §4.2
E4 · V4 storage base slot · $\mathrm{slot} = \mathrm{keccak256}(\mathrm{abi.encode}(\mathrm{poolId}, 6))$; $\sqrt{P}$ in bits [0,160), LP fee in [208,232) of word 0; $L$ in word 3 · defined in Core `v4SqrtAndLiq` · §5
E5 · Solidly stable invariant · $k(x,y) = x^{3}y + xy^{3}$ · defined in Core `_solK` · §6
E6 · Solidly Newton step · seed $y_{0} = Y$; up-step $\max(1, \lfloor (K-k)/f' \rfloor)$; down-step $\max(1, \lfloor (k-K)/f' \rfloor)$, replaced by $\lfloor y/2 \rfloor$ when it would cross zero; exit at $\lvert y_{n+1}-y_{n}\rvert \le 1$ with a one-unit bump against the taker; cap 64 → seed → quote 0 · defined in Core `_solY` · §6
E7 · Decimal normalisation · $X = r_{\mathrm{in}}10^{18-d_{\mathrm{in}}}$, $Y = r_{\mathrm{out}}10^{18-d_{\mathrm{out}}}$, de-scaled after the solve · defined in Core `_solidlyStable` · §6
E8 · CREATE2 derivation · $\mathrm{pool} = \mathrm{addr}_{20}(\mathrm{keccak256}(\mathtt{0xff} \Vert \mathrm{origin} \Vert \mathrm{salt} \Vert \mathrm{initCodeHash}))$ · defined in Core `create2Address`, `deriveAddress` · §7
E9 · Monoslot packing · $s = a \,\vert\, f\!\ll\!8 \,\vert\, k\!\ll\!32 \,\vert\, r\!\ll\!40 \,\vert\, (c\wedge\mathtt{0xFFF})\!\ll\!48 \,\vert\, b\!\ll\!60 \,\vert\, \dots \,\vert\, B_{\mathrm{last}}\!\ll\!224$ · defined in Core `encodeSlot` · §8
E10 · Vitality Field · $\Psi = V \cdot 2^{b} \cdot (1 + 0.25\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{bridge}}) \cdot (1 + 0.05\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{conc}})$ · defined in Core `psi` · §9.2
E11 · Activity decay · $V = \mathrm{swapCount} \gg \lfloor (t - t_{\mathrm{last}})/24{,}576 \rfloor$; 0 once the shift exceeds 31 · defined in Core `_decayedSwapCount` · §9.2
E12 · Depth bucket · $b = \min(15, \lfloor \log_{10}(d/10^{15}) \rfloor)$ · defined in Core `depthBucket` · §9.2
E13 · Eviction hurdle · $2^{b(d_{\mathrm{new}})} > \Psi_{\mathrm{worst}} + \lfloor \Psi_{\mathrm{worst}}/4 \rfloor$ · defined in Hub `_canInsert` · §9.3
E14 · Split gate · keep the split iff $\mathrm{out}_{\mathrm{split}} \ge \mathrm{out}_{\mathrm{single}}\cdot(1 + 25/10^{6})$, $\mathrm{out}_{\mathrm{single}}$ the better of the deepest and the best-rate candidate at full size · defined in Solver `_buildHop` · §10.4
E15 · Iron-Law floor · $\mathtt{floorBps} = \max(9{,}600 - \mathtt{legShv} - \min(\delta, 10^{4}) - \sigma_{\ln}/10^{14},\ 8{,}000)$ · defined in Core `ironFloorBpsShv` · §11.5
E16 · Effective minimum · $\mathtt{effMin} = \max(\mathtt{userMinOut},\ \mathtt{route.singleOutFloor},\ \lceil \mathtt{finalHopQuote}\cdot\mathtt{floorBps}/10^{4}\rceil)$; the second term dropped and the third re-scaled by the measured net ratio when fee-on-transfer is detected · defined in Router `_execute` · §11.5
E17 · Protocol fee · $\mathrm{fee} = \lceil 28 \cdot \mathrm{base} / 10^{4} \rceil$, base = the fee hop's measured input (anchored), the gross output (direct route into a bridge coin), or each hop's measured input (exhaustion); $t_{1} = \lfloor 3{,}000\cdot\mathrm{fee}/10^{4} \rfloor$, $t_{2} = \mathrm{fee} - t_{1}$ · defined in Router `_chargeHopFee`, `_payFee` · §13
E18 · Hook gate · $(\mathrm{uint160}(\mathrm{hook}) \,\&\, \mathtt{0x3FFF}) \,\&\, ((1\ll 3)\mid(1\ll 2)) \ne 0 \Rightarrow$ leg refused, no call made · defined in Core `hookAltersDeltas`; Router · §14.2
E19 · Dynamic-fee gate · $f_{\mathrm{eff}} = f_{\mathrm{key}}$ if static; unquotable if the sentinel rides with a non-zero protocol fee; else the live LP fee from `slot0` / `globalState` / the pool's `fee()` · defined in Core `effV4Fee`, `quoteV3Fee` · §5.4
E20 · V2 fee ceiling · $f_{\mathrm{eff}} = f_{\mathrm{decl}}$ if $0 < f_{\mathrm{decl}} \le 100$ bps, else 30 · defined in Core `effV2Fee`; the same rule for the Solidly declared fallback · §4.2
E21 · Preview safety buffer · $s = \min(\max(0, n-2) + 5a,\ 10)$ bps · defined in Quoter `_pack` · §12.1
E22 · Surface choice · carry the route in calldata iff $p_{\mathrm{byte}} < \rho^{*}$; $\rho^{*}$ measured 66.9–105.5 gas/byte by route shape · defined in `test/EquationBench.t.sol` · §17.6
E23 · Leg shave from concentration · $\mathtt{legShv} = \sum_{\mathrm{hops}} \lfloor 200\,((\sum a)^{2} - \sum a^{2})/\sum a^{2} \rfloor$ · defined in Core `legShaveBps` · §11.5
E24 · Aggregate hop floor · $\sum \mathrm{got} + \lfloor (\mathrm{BPS} - 8{,}000)\cdot \lfloor \sum \mathrm{attested}/n \rfloor / \mathrm{BPS} \rfloor \ge \sum \mathrm{attested}$ · defined in Router `_execute` · §11.3
E25 · Believability centre · the depth-weighted median: sort $(r_{i}, d_{i})$ by $r_{i}$, return the first $r_{i}$ at which $\sum_{j \le i} d_{j} \ge \lceil \sum d / 2 \rceil$; band $[0.95, 1.05] \times$ centre · defined in Solver `_depthWeightedMedian` · §10.3
E26 · Fee regime predicate · $\mathrm{feeHop} = \min\{h : \mathrm{isBridge}(\mathrm{hops}[h].\mathrm{tokenIn})\}$; charge at $h$ iff $\neg\mathrm{feeOnOut} \wedge (\mathrm{feeHop} = \infty \vee h = \mathrm{feeHop})$; $\mathrm{feeOnOut} \iff$ one hop and $\mathrm{isBridge}(\mathrm{tokenOut})$ · defined in Router `_execute` · §13.1

## Appendix B — the invariants (INV-1–INV-22), each enforced by the shape of the code at the site named
INV-1 · The Router holds no funds between transactions; its balance at rest is zero. · enforced by Baseline-scoped sweeps and payout (§11); `invariant_RouterHoldsNothing`, `HoldsNothingBeyondTheSeed`
INV-2 · Every swap is atomic: no state exists in which part of a trade settled. · enforced by EVM transaction semantics; one frame
INV-3 · No oracle: no external price feed is an input to admission, ordering, splitting, flooring or fees. · enforced by No feed call exists in the five contracts
INV-4 · The fee rate, the fee split and the floor constants have no setters in the deployed bytecode. · enforced by Compile-time constants in the Core and the Router (§13)
INV-5 · Caller-supplied route fields can tighten protection, never loosen it. · enforced by E16 three-way maximum; the coverage gate lifts an attestation, never lowers it (§11)
INV-6 · A swap with a zero minimum does not execute. · enforced by `RouterE(10)` at every door
INV-7 · Ψ ranks and truncates candidates; no quote, floor or allocation reads it. · enforced by Data flow: nothing downstream of ranking consumes Ψ (§9.6)
INV-8 · A pair's registry holds at most sixteen pools, and eviction keeps the fittest by full Ψ with the margin of E13. · enforced by Hub `_canInsert`; `invariant_neverExceedsMaxSlots` (the cap); `test_RecordSwap_EvictsWeakestWhenFullAndNewcomerClearsMargin` (the eviction)
INV-9 · No address without runtime bytecode enters a route. · enforced by `hasCode` on every derivation (§7)
INV-10 · The universal callback pays only the pool committed for the current leg, only while a leg is in flight, and never more than the leg's recorded budget. · enforced by Transient leg context; `RouterE(6)` for the pool, `RouterE(8)` for the budget (§11.4)
INV-11 · A V4 hook whose address declares delta-altering permissions is rejected before any token moves, without calling it. · enforced by E18; `RouterE(9)`; Solver `_topKPools`
INV-12 · No pricing product can overflow: every dangerous multiplication is factored through 512-bit `mulDiv`, and a state that cannot be bounded quotes zero. · enforced by Core (§4.2, §6)
INV-13 · Rounding runs against over-promise: quotes and payouts floor, protective floors and the fee round up. · enforced by Core `mulDiv` / `mulDivUp` at each site
INV-14 · Where a bound cannot be proven, the computation returns zero and the venue is surrendered — never a guess, never a schedulable revert inside a quote. · enforced by Fail-closed posture across the Core; `_solKFits` (§6)
INV-15 · The fee base is the measured pull, capped by the route's committed input — never a declared output; `route.totalOut` is read by nothing. · enforced by `_chargeHopFee`; `test_FeeBase_IgnoresLiedAboutTotalOut`
INV-16 · Renunciation is one-way: the flag is written `true` at one site and `false` at none; after it, only the grow-only curator tier remains, and a moved factory or hook cannot be re-armed. · enforced by `renounceControl` on Hub and Router (§14.7)
INV-17 · A declared constant-product or Solidly fallback fee is believed only within a 100 bps ceiling; outside it the canonical 30 bps prices the pool. · enforced by E20
INV-18 · No hop carries more than four legs and no route more than eleven in the Solver's plan; the Router accepts at most three hops and five legs per hop. · enforced by Solver budgets; Router `_execute` → `RouterE(3)`
INV-19 · A pool enters the registry only if it proves it trades the pair: `token0()`/`token1()` for pair-shaped kinds, re-derivation of the pool id for V4; an asked pool proves the same before discovery lists it. · enforced by Hub `recordSwap`, `_probe`; `invariant_ActiveEntriesTradeThePair`
INV-20 · A settlement pays the protocol fee exactly once on an anchored route and once per hop on an exhausted one; a settlement that paid nothing does not exist. · enforced by Fee ledger, `RouterE(15)`/`RouterE(16)`; `invariant_SettledSwapEmitsExactlyOneFee` (anchored); `test/FeeSeals.t.sol`, `test/ExhaustionRegimePreviewParity.t.sol` (exhaustion)
INV-21 · Hops chain — each hop's input is the previous hop's output — and no hookless leg executes after a hooked one, in this or any later hop (`sawHooked` is route-wide). · enforced by Router `_execute` → `RouterE(3)`; `sawHooked`
INV-22 · The four deployed contracts — Hub, Solver, Router, Quoter — ship under the project's 24,000-byte gate on the release profile, the Core library is measured separately (6,477 bytes of 24,576), and the suite runs on that profile. · enforced by `DeployedSizeGate`; `profile_parity.py`
